subtype: Angry and irritated in shared living and study [Regulating]
passage: Hostel warden's note. Over the past two weeks Gargi has come to my office three times about her roommate Neelam's music, late lights and unwashed cups. On each visit she said less and her voice got tighter. This week she told me she was starting to snap at Neelam in front of others. I asked what she wanted to be different, and she said she just wanted quiet after ten. I suggested she tell Neelam calmly and early, when she's not annoyed, and take a short walk if she feels angry. She agreed to try that evening. Two days later, she mentioned it went better than she expected. Neelam turned her music down and apologised. I will check in next week.

qa.q: How many times had Gargi come to the warden's office?
qa.a: She had come three times in two weeks.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling as her visits went on, and what did she want?
qa.a: She was growing irritated, with a tighter voice each time, and she wanted quiet after ten.

qa.q: What worked for Gargi in handling the conflict?
qa.a: She told Neelam calmly and early and took a walk when angry, and Neelam responded by turning her music down.

qa.q: How might Neelam have felt when Gargi spoke to her calmly?
qa.a: Neelam may have been surprised and a bit embarrassed, since she apologised and turned her music down.

grounding: A warden's note shows Gargi naming an irritation early, staying calm and taking breaks with her roommate Neelam.

subtype: Angry and irritated in shared living and study [Regulating]
passage: Thursday, 10:40 pm. Our group project meeting ran late, and Baljeet still hasn't sent his part. Third time this month. I'm Lokesh, and I felt my face get hot when he said, "Oh, it's nearly done." I wanted to say something cutting. Instead I said, "I need to step out for a few minutes," and I walked to the corridor and counted my breaths by the window. When I came back, I said, "Can we agree on a time for your section? Tomorrow at noon?" He nodded. His reply was quieter than usual, and I don't know if he was embarrassed or annoyed. Either way, we now have a time. I might message him later that I'm not upset about him personally.

qa.q: How many times this month had Baljeet been late?
qa.a: This was the third time this month.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when Baljeet said it was nearly done, and how did Lokesh handle it?
qa.a: Lokesh felt irritated, with a hot face, and stepped out to calm down instead of saying something cutting.

qa.q: What could Lokesh do next to keep the group working well?
qa.a: Lokesh could message Baljeet that the irritation is not about Baljeet personally and check that noon works.

qa.q: How might Baljeet have felt when Lokesh set a time?
qa.a: Baljeet may have felt embarrassed or pressured, or maybe just tired, since his reply was quieter than usual and the diary can't tell which.

grounding: Lokesh notices irritation building over a late group section and uses a break and a calm request.

subtype: Angry and irritated in shared living and study [Regulating]
passage: The group project at the polytechnic in Hoshangabad was due in ten days, and Kamal had missed three meetings. Each time Kiran sent a message; each time Kamal replied, "Sorry, coming next time." By the fourth meeting, Kiran felt the anger building: jaw tight, words sharp in her head. She almost typed, "You're useless." Instead she walked twice round the college ground, bought a lime soda, and waited till her breathing slowed. Then she called him. "Kamal, I'm frustrated. We've met four times and you've come to none. I need to know if you can do the wiring section by Friday, or if we should split it differently." There was a pause. "My father's shop assistant quit. I've been at the counter every evening." Kiran's anger softened. "Can you do mornings?" "Yes." "Then let's meet at eight tomorrow." He came, and did his part.

qa.q: How many meetings had Kamal missed before Kiran called?
qa.a: Three meetings; he had come to none of the four.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling before she called Kamal?
qa.a: She was angry and frustrated, her jaw tight and harsh words in her head.

qa.q: What helped Kiran avoid turning irritation into a fight?
qa.a: Taking a break to walk and calm down, then naming the issue calmly with a clear request.

qa.q: What was Kamal dealing with that Kiran didn't know?
qa.a: His father's shop assistant had quit, so he had been working at the counter every evening.

grounding: Shows a young adult calming building anger with a break and naming a group project issue in calm words before it becomes conflict.

subtype: Angry and irritated in shared living and study [Regulating]
passage: Nkechi had been sharing a flat in London with Wanjiru for two months, and the late-night phone calls were wearing her down. Every night, past midnight, Wanjiru's laugh came through the thin wall. Nkechi lay awake, getting angrier, rehearsing a speech. One morning she caught herself slamming the kettle down. That scared her. She didn't want to be the person who slammed things. So that evening, when they were both cooking, she said, "Can I mention something small before it becomes big? The calls after midnight wake me up, and I've got early shifts. Could you take them in the kitchen after twelve, or keep them shorter?" Wanjiru winced. "Oh no, I didn't realise the wall was that thin. My family's in Nairobi, it's the only time they're free." "The kitchen, then?" "The kitchen. And I'll use earphones." That night, Nkechi slept through.

qa.q: Where is Wanjiru's family?
qa.a: In Nairobi.

qa.q: What was Nkechi feeling before she spoke up?
qa.a: She was angry and worn down from lost sleep, and scared by how she slammed the kettle.

qa.q: Why was raising it early and calmly a good choice?
qa.a: It let Nkechi explain the problem before anger took over, and they found a simple fix together.

qa.q: How did Wanjiru react to Nkechi's request?
qa.a: She winced, apologised for not realising the wall was thin, explained her family's timing, and agreed to use the kitchen and earphones.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing irritation building in shared living and naming the issue early with calm words.

subtype: Angry and irritated in shared living and study [Regulating]
passage: By the second week in the engineering college hostel, Tarun had counted it: Chetan's speaker came on at eleven-thirty every night, bass thumping through the bunk. On Monday Tarun pulled his pillow over his head. On Tuesday he slammed his cupboard door, hoping that would say it for him. It didn't. On Wednesday, lying awake at one, he caught himself drafting a furious speech in his head, words he knew he'd regret. So he got up, walked to the common room, drank a glass of water, and wrote down what he actually needed. On Thursday afternoon, when both of them were relaxed, he said, "Can I bring up something small before it becomes big? The music after eleven is keeping me up, and I've got eight o'clock labs." Chetan blinked. "Seriously? Why didn't you say? I thought you liked it." They settled on headphones after eleven, and Tarun's cupboard door stayed quiet.

qa.q: What time did Chetan's speaker come on each night?
qa.a: At eleven-thirty.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling by Wednesday night?
qa.a: Tarun's irritation had built into real anger, enough to draft a furious speech he knew he'd regret.

qa.q: What stopped the irritation turning into a fight?
qa.a: Taking a break to walk and write down the need, then raising it early and calmly at a relaxed moment with a specific request.

qa.q: How had Chetan read Tarun's silence and the slammed door?
qa.a: He hadn't understood them at all; he thought Tarun liked the music.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult noticing irritation building with a roommate, taking a break, and naming the issue early in calm words before it becomes conflict.
